appId: com.betweenus.desktop
productName: BetweenUs
electronVersion: 31.3.1
directories:
  output: release
files:
  - dist/**
  - dist-electron/**
  - public/icon.png
# Release artifacts are named BetweenUs-<version>-<what it is>, the same shape
# the Android APKs use, so a downloaded file still says which release it is and
# a folder of them sorts by version rather than by target.
#
# One Windows target, and it is the installer. There was a portable exe beside
# it until the two of them turned every update into a question of which build
# somebody was running - and the answer was wrong often enough that neither
# updated reliably. See development/devdocs/UPDATES.md.
win:
  target:
    - nsis
  icon: public/icon.png
nsis:
  artifactName: BetweenUs-${version}-Setup.${ext}
  # Both places electron-builder starts the app go through StdUtils, which is
  # for de-elevating a launch this installer never needs to. See nsis/installer
  # .nsh and development/devdocs/UPDATES.md. Named explicitly rather than left
  # in the build resources: `build/` is gitignored, so a file there would exist
  # on one machine and never reach a release.
  include: nsis/installer.nsh
  # An assisted installer, not a one-click one: somebody installing BetweenUs
  # for the first time gets to say where it goes, and gets a licence-free
  # wizard they can read rather than a progress bar that has already finished.
  oneClick: false
  allowToChangeInstallationDirectory: true
  # Per user, so no UAC prompt and no administrator to find. An update started
  # by the app itself runs as the user who is signed in, and a per-machine
  # install would ask that user for a password they may not have.
  perMachine: false
  allowElevation: false
  createDesktopShortcut: true
  createStartMenuShortcut: true
  shortcutName: BetweenUs
  menuCategory: false
  runAfterFinish: true
  # The account's messages, keys and settings live in AppData. Uninstalling to
  # reinstall is a thing people do, and it must not be what loses their keys.
  deleteAppDataOnUninstall: false
  uninstallDisplayName: BetweenUs ${version}
mac:
  target: dmg
  icon: public/icon.png
  artifactName: BetweenUs-${version}.${ext}
linux:
  target: AppImage
  icon: public/icon.png
  artifactName: BetweenUs-${version}.${ext}

/**
 * Shortcodes for the curated set, so `:` can find one by name.
 *
 * `emoji.ts` said that shipping the whole Unicode set with a search index was
 * the moment to add a dependency, and that this was not that moment. It still
 * is not: what a `:` menu needs is a name per emoji *this app already draws*,
 * which is this table - about six kilobytes of text against the ~1.5 MB an
 * emoji package brings, and it works offline, in an Electron package, with no
 * sprite sheet to load.
 *
 * The format is one `emoji:name` per entry, whitespace-separated, with extra
 * aliases appended after further colons - `👍:thumbsup:+1:yes`. It is written
 * as text rather than an object literal because a 450-entry object is a 450-
 * line diff every time one is added, and because the parse is four lines.
 *
 * Names follow the shortcodes people already have in their fingers from
 * Slack, GitHub and Discord, which mostly agree with each other. Where they
 * disagree, both are listed: nobody should have to learn which of the three
 * this app copied.
 */

export interface NamedEmoji {
  emoji: string;
  /** The first name is the one shown; the rest are aliases that also match. */
  names: string[];
}

/** The table, parsed once. */
export const NAMED_EMOJI: NamedEmoji[] = TABLE.trim()
  .split(/\s+/)
  .flatMap((entry) => {
    const [emoji, ...names] = entry.split(':');
    // An entry with no name is a typo in the table above, not a thing to draw.
    if (!emoji || names.length === 0) return [];
    return [{ emoji, names }];
  });

/** How many suggestions a `:` menu shows. More than this is a scroll, not a menu. */
export const EMOJI_SUGGESTION_LIMIT = 8;

/**
 * Emoji whose name matches what has been typed so far.
 *
 * Ranked, because the order is the whole usefulness of a menu that shows eight
 * of four hundred: an exact name first, then names that start with the term,
 * then names that merely contain it. Without that, `:fire` offers
 * `fire_engine` above 🔥, which is the sort of thing that makes people stop
 * using a feature rather than report it.
 */
export function searchEmoji(term: string, limit = EMOJI_SUGGESTION_LIMIT): NamedEmoji[] {
  const needle = term.trim().toLowerCase().replace(/^:+/, '');
  if (needle.length === 0) return [];

  const scored: Array<{ entry: NamedEmoji; rank: number }> = [];

  for (const entry of NAMED_EMOJI) {
    let best = Infinity;
    for (const name of entry.names) {
      if (name === needle) best = Math.min(best, 0);
      else if (name.startsWith(needle)) best = Math.min(best, 1);
      else if (name.includes(needle)) best = Math.min(best, 2);
    }
    if (best !== Infinity) scored.push({ entry, rank: best });
  }

  // A stable sort by rank keeps the table's own order inside each rank, which
  // is roughly most-common-first because that is how the groups were written.
  return scored
    .sort((left, right) => left.rank - right.rank)
    .slice(0, limit)
    .map((row) => row.entry);
}

/**
 * The `:term` being typed at the caret, if there is one.
 *
 * Returns where it starts as well as the term, because replacing it needs both.
 * Null for everything that is not one, and the exclusions are the whole of the
 * work here: a colon in `https://` or in `10:30` must not open a menu, and a
 * colon that has already been closed - `:tada:` - is a finished shortcode
 * rather than a search in progress.
 */
export function emojiQueryAt(text: string, caret: number): { term: string; start: number } | null {
  const before = text.slice(0, caret);
  const colon = before.lastIndexOf(':');
  if (colon === -1) return null;

  const term = before.slice(colon + 1);
  // A space ends it: `:` on its own, then a word, is not one shortcode.
  if (/[\s:]/.test(term)) return null;
  // Two characters before anything is offered - `:` alone would show a menu
  // over every URL somebody types.
  if (term.length < 2) return null;
  if (!/^[a-z0-9_+-]+$/i.test(term)) return null;

  // What precedes the colon decides whether it is a shortcode at all. Start of
  // line or after whitespace is one; `https:` and `10:` are not.
  const preceding = colon === 0 ? '' : (before[colon - 1] ?? '');
  if (preceding !== '' && !/\s/.test(preceding)) return null;

  return { term, start: colon };
}

/**
 * What the tray draws when nobody has posted.
 *
 * A drawing rather than the sentence that used to be here: an empty screen
 * with one grey line on it reads as something that failed to load. Inline SVG
 * rather than a file, for the same reason every other icon in the app is - it
 * inherits the text colour, so it is right in both themes without a second

 * The ring is segmented like the one an avatar wears when there is something

/**
 * When to try a broken link again, and when to stop trying.
 *
 * The web and Electron clients had none of this: one `restartIce()` the moment
 * ICE said `failed`, and then the peer was dropped out of the mesh for good.
 * Nothing re-adds a link, so a single bad moment on either end - a wifi
 * handover, a laptop lid, a candidate pair that lost a race - ended that pair
 * for the rest of the call, and the only cure was leaving and rejoining. That
 * is the "have to drop and join a few times" everybody was doing.
 *
 * Android already had a policy for exactly this, in `CallRecovery.kt`, and this
 * is that policy in TypeScript. It is deliberately a straight port rather than
 * a second opinion: two clients that disagree about how long to wait before an
 * ICE restart are two clients that restart on top of each other, and a
 * renegotiation racing another renegotiation is worse than either alone. Every
 * number here is a trade between two failures that both look like a bug: giving
 * up on a link that would have come back, and pretending for a minute that a
 * call is still alive when it is not.
 *
 * Pure, so it can be reasoned about - and checked - without a call. See
 * `call-recovery.check.ts`.
 */

/**
 * How long a `disconnected` link is left alone before anything is done.
 *
 * ICE recovers by itself surprisingly often - a lost packet or two on a
 * handover puts a connection here and it climbs out unaided within a couple of
 * seconds. Restarting immediately would throw away a link that was about to be
 * fine, and an ICE restart is not free: it is a renegotiation, and on a bad
 * network it is a renegotiation over the network that is bad.
 */
export const GRACE_MS = 4_000;

/** How many ICE restarts one link gets before it is declared lost. */
export const MAX_ATTEMPTS = 4;

/**
 * The longest a link may spend not carrying media before it is given up on,
 * whatever the attempt count says.
 *
 * Half a minute of a frozen tile is already longer than anybody waits before
 * saying "I think you've frozen" - past that it is kinder to say so than to
 * keep a hopeful spinner up.
 */
export const DEADLINE_MS = 30_000;

/**
 * How long the whole call survives with no signalling.
 *
 * Longer than one link's deadline on purpose: the socket reconnects itself and
 * rejoins, and a train tunnel is a real thing that ends. But a call whose
 * switchboard has been unreachable for this long is a call nobody else can see
 * this device in - the roster dropped it long ago - so keeping the microphone
 * open is a lie told to its owner.
 */
export const SIGNALLING_DEADLINE_MS = 45_000;

/**
 * Which side restarts ICE.
 *
 * The impolite one, and only it. An ICE restart has to become an offer to do
 * anything at all, and only the impolite side offers unprompted - that is the
 * whole of the perfect-negotiation rule this call already follows. The polite
 * side calling `restartIce()` marks its connection as wanting a renegotiation
 * that the impolite side will discard as glare, which looks like a recovery
 * attempt in a log and is not one.
 *
 * So the polite side waits. If the impolite side is alive it will offer; if it
 * is not, the roster is what says so.
 */
export function restarts(polite: boolean): boolean {
  return !polite;
}

/**
 * How long to wait before attempt `attempt`, counting from one.
 *
 * Backed off, because the reason the first restart failed is usually that the
 * network is still bad, and four restarts inside a second is four
 * renegotiations that all fail together. Capped so the last attempt still
 * happens inside `DEADLINE_MS`.
 */
export function backoffMs(attempt: number): number {
  if (attempt <= 1) return 0;
  if (attempt === 2) return 2_000;
  if (attempt === 3) return 4_000;
  return 8_000;
}

/**
 * Whether a link that has been down for `downForMs` across `attempts` restarts
 * should be given up on.
 *
 * Either bound is enough. The attempt count catches a link that is failing fast
 * and repeatedly; the deadline catches one that is failing slowly, or that
 * never reports a failure at all and simply sits in `disconnected`.
 */
export function spent(attempts: number, downForMs: number): boolean {
  return attempts >= MAX_ATTEMPTS || downForMs >= DEADLINE_MS;
}

/**
 * How long to wait before the nth attempt at reopening the signalling socket.
 *
 * The gateway holds a departed peer's seat for a grace window (see
 * `resumeHeldSeat` in `call.gateway.ts`), so a socket that comes back quickly
 * rejoins the call it was already in and nobody else is told anything happened.
 * That window is the thing worth racing, which is why the first retry is
 * immediate; after that it backs off, because a server that refused once will
 * usually refuse again a second later.
 *
 * Capped below `SIGNALLING_DEADLINE_MS` so the last attempt lands inside it.
 */
export function signallingBackoffMs(attempt: number): number {
  if (attempt <= 1) return 0;
  return Math.min(1_000 * 2 ** (attempt - 2), 8_000);
}

/**
 * Whether a peer's camera or screen is on.
 *
 * There are two signals about a remote video slot and they answer different
 * questions, which is the mistake this exists to stop anyone making again.
 *
 * *Frames decoded* say whether a picture is arriving right now. They are the
 * only honest signal for that: a video receiver unmutes on the padding sent to
 * probe for bandwidth, so a track that never carried anything looks live. What
 * they do NOT say is whether the far end is still sharing - a screen share of a
 * document nobody is typing in decodes no frames for minutes at a time, and it
 * is still very much a share.
 *
 * *The declared media state*, which every client publishes over the peer's data
 * channel whenever it turns something on or off, is the answer to "are they
 * sharing". It is a statement of intent from the only party that knows.
 *
 * Deciding existence from frames is what made a viewer open somebody's share,
 * watch a still screen for five seconds, and be dropped back to the grid with
 * an offer to watch it again.
 */

/**
 * The track to show for one slot: what has arrived, unless its owner says that
 * slot is off.
 *
 * `declared` is `undefined` for the moment between a track arriving and the
 * peer's first media state landing - and for any client that publishes none.
 * There, what arrived is the best answer available, which is what this used to
 * do all the time.
 */
export function visibleVideo<T>(declared: boolean | undefined, arrived: T | null): T | null {
  if (!arrived) return null;
  return declared === false ? null : arrived;
}

/**
 * Which runtime this UI is running in.
 *
 * The same React source builds two clients: the Electron app in `apps/desktop`
 * and the browser bundle in `apps/web`. Everything that needs a machine - screen
 * capture by source, synthetic mouse and keyboard input, the OS keychain - is
 * behind the preload bridge, and a browser has none of it. So the split is not a
 * build flag but the bridge's own presence: one bundle, and the parts that
 * cannot work in a tab are not offered there.
 *
 * What this gates is the *remote desktop* section - the machine list, the agent
 * that offers this machine, and the Remote Access settings. Asking for control
 * of somebody's screen share inside a call is not gated: sending input events
 * over the data channel needs no bridge, and the machine on the other end is the
 * one that has to be able to apply them (see stores/shareControl.ts).
 */

/** True in the Electron app, false in a browser tab. */
export function isDesktopRuntime(): boolean {
  return typeof window !== 'undefined' && window.betweenus !== undefined;
}

/**
 * Applying WebRTC signals one at a time.
 *
 * Every negotiator here takes signals off a socket that does not wait for them:
 * the handler is `void`ed or launched, so two descriptions arriving close
 * together run *concurrently* and interleave at every `await` inside. That
 * breaks perfect negotiation at the root, because the decisions it makes -
 * "is this a collision", "is there still an offer outstanding" - are read from
 * `signalingState` and then acted on several awaits later, by which time
 * another run has moved the connection on.
 *
 * The symptom is an offer and a re-offer from the connection chaser landing
 * together: both pass the collision check while the state is still
 * `have-remote-offer`, the first drives the connection to `stable` with its
 * answer, and the second reaches `setLocalDescription('answer')` a moment later
 * and throws `Called in wrong state: stable` across a call that is otherwise
 * fine.
 *
 * One queue per peer, never one per mesh: separate connections share no state,
 * and queueing them behind each other would make the slowest peer's key re-read
 * everybody else's problem.
 */

/**
 * A queue that runs each task to completion before starting the next.
 *
 * Rejections are swallowed rather than propagated into the chain: one failed
 * signal must not stop every signal after it, which is a call that goes quiet
 * for good. Callers that care about the outcome handle it inside the task, as
 * both negotiators do.
 */
export function serialize(): (task: () => Promise<void>) => Promise<void> {
  let tail: Promise<void> = Promise.resolve();
  return (task) => {
    tail = tail.then(task).catch(() => undefined);
    return tail;
  };
}

const STORAGE_KEY = 'betweenus.theme-settings';

export interface ThemeSettings {
  selectedTheme: ThemeId;
  followSystem: boolean;
  customAccentId: string;
  /**
   * How tightly the conversation is packed. Appearance, so it lives with the
   * theme rather than in a store of its own - and is persisted the same way,
   * per machine, because it is about this screen at this sitting distance.
   */
  density: Density;
  /**
   * The language, and with it which way the layout runs.
   *
   * Here rather than on the account for the same reason density is: it is about
   * the machine in front of somebody, and the person who reads English at work
   * and Arabic at home should not have to change one to change the other.
   *
   * Nothing is translated yet. What this changes today is `lang` and `dir` on
   * the document, which is the half that had to exist before any string was
   * worth extracting - and the half that is worth nothing if a component was
   * written with a physical margin, which is what `i18n.check.ts` holds.
   */
  locale: Locale;
}

const DEFAULT_SETTINGS: ThemeSettings = {
  selectedTheme: 'dark',
  followSystem: false,
  customAccentId: 'default',
  density: 'cozy',
  // The machine's own language, not `en`. Somebody whose system is set to
  // Arabic gets a right-to-left layout on first launch without being asked,
  // which is what every other application on their machine does.
  locale: typeof navigator === 'undefined' ? 'en' : preferredLocale(navigator.languages ?? []),
};

function getSystemPrefersDark(): boolean {
  if (typeof window === 'undefined' || !window.matchMedia) return true;
  return window.matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').matches;
}

function resolveEffectiveTheme(settings: ThemeSettings): ThemeId {
  if (settings.followSystem) {
    const isDark = getSystemPrefersDark();
    if (!isDark) return 'light';
    // If system is dark, respect user's picked dark theme or default dark
    return settings.selectedTheme === 'light' ? 'dark' : settings.selectedTheme;
  }
  return settings.selectedTheme;
}

function applyThemeToDocument(resolvedThemeId: ThemeId, customAccentId: string): void {
  if (typeof document === 'undefined') return;

  const themeDef = THEMES[resolvedThemeId] ?? THEMES.dark;
  const targets = [document.documentElement, document.body].filter(Boolean) as HTMLElement[];

  for (const target of targets) {
    target.setAttribute('data-theme', themeDef.id);
    target.style.colorScheme = themeDef.type;

    // Apply CSS color variables
    for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(themeDef.colors)) {
      target.style.setProperty(key, value);
    }

    // If a custom accent was chosen, override the accent variables
    const accent = ACCENT_PRESETS.find((preset) => preset.id === customAccentId);
    if (accent && accent.value) {
      target.style.setProperty('--color-accent', accent.value);
      target.style.setProperty('--color-accent-hover', accent.hover);
    } else {
      // Revert to theme's defined accent
      target.style.setProperty('--color-accent', themeDef.colors['--color-accent'] ?? '124 92 255');
      target.style.setProperty('--color-accent-hover', themeDef.colors['--color-accent-hover'] ?? '106 68 245');
    }
  }

  // Update native window titlebar controls overlay (Windows hidden titlebar)
  if (typeof window !== 'undefined' && window.betweenus?.setTitleBarOverlay) {
    window.betweenus.setTitleBarOverlay(themeDef.titleBarOverlay);
  }
}

function loadSettings(): ThemeSettings {
  try {
    const raw = localStorage.getItem(STORAGE_KEY);
    if (!raw) return DEFAULT_SETTINGS;
    const parsed = JSON.parse(raw) as Partial<ThemeSettings>;
    return {
      selectedTheme: parsed.selectedTheme && THEMES[parsed.selectedTheme] ? parsed.selectedTheme : 'dark',
      followSystem: Boolean(parsed.followSystem),
      customAccentId: parsed.customAccentId ?? 'default',
      density: asDensity(parsed.density),
      locale: parsed.locale === undefined ? DEFAULT_SETTINGS.locale : asLocale(parsed.locale),
    };
  } catch {
    return DEFAULT_SETTINGS;
  }
}

interface ThemeState {
  settings: ThemeSettings;
  resolvedTheme: ThemeId;
  setTheme: (themeId: ThemeId) => void;
  setFollowSystem: (follow: boolean) => void;
  setCustomAccent: (accentId: string) => void;
  setDensity: (density: Density) => void;
  /** The language, and the direction that comes with it. */
  setInterfaceLocale: (locale: Locale) => void;
}

export const useThemeStore = create<ThemeState>((set, get) => ({
  settings: loadSettings(),
  resolvedTheme: resolveEffectiveTheme(loadSettings()),

  setTheme: (themeId: ThemeId) => {
    const nextSettings: ThemeSettings = {
      ...get().settings,
      selectedTheme: themeId,
      followSystem: false, // Explicit theme click disables followSystem
    };
    const resolved = resolveEffectiveTheme(nextSettings);
    set({ settings: nextSettings, resolvedTheme: resolved });
    try {
      localStorage.setItem(STORAGE_KEY, JSON.stringify(nextSettings));
    } catch {}
    applyThemeToDocument(resolved, nextSettings.customAccentId);
  },

  setFollowSystem: (follow: boolean) => {
    const nextSettings: ThemeSettings = {
      ...get().settings,
      followSystem: follow,
    };
    const resolved = resolveEffectiveTheme(nextSettings);
    set({ settings: nextSettings, resolvedTheme: resolved });
    try {
      localStorage.setItem(STORAGE_KEY, JSON.stringify(nextSettings));
    } catch {}
    applyThemeToDocument(resolved, nextSettings.customAccentId);
  },

  setCustomAccent: (accentId: string) => {
    const nextSettings: ThemeSettings = {
      ...get().settings,
      customAccentId: accentId,
    };
    set({ settings: nextSettings });
    try {
      localStorage.setItem(STORAGE_KEY, JSON.stringify(nextSettings));
    } catch {}
    applyThemeToDocument(get().resolvedTheme, nextSettings.customAccentId);
  },

  /**
   * Cozy or compact. Nothing about the document changes - density is spacing
   * inside the message list rather than a variable on `:root` - so this only
   * stores the choice and lets the list re-render.
   */
  setDensity: (density: Density) => {
    const nextSettings: ThemeSettings = { ...get().settings, density };
    set({ settings: nextSettings });
    try {
      localStorage.setItem(STORAGE_KEY, JSON.stringify(nextSettings));
    } catch {}
  },

  setInterfaceLocale: (locale: Locale) => {
    const nextSettings: ThemeSettings = { ...get().settings, locale };
    set({ settings: nextSettings });
    // The document is pointed here rather than by an effect somewhere, so that
    // the one call that changes the setting is the one call that changes the
    // screen - the same shape `setTheme` uses.
    setLocale(locale);
    try {
      localStorage.setItem(STORAGE_KEY, JSON.stringify(nextSettings));
    } catch {}
  },
}));

/**
 * Initialize theme immediately at bootstrap and set up OS color scheme change listener.
 */
export function initTheme(): () => void {
  const initial = loadSettings();
  const resolved = resolveEffectiveTheme(initial);
  applyThemeToDocument(resolved, initial.customAccentId);
  // Before React mounts, for the same reason the theme is: a document that
  // starts left-to-right and turns over once the app has painted is a visible
  // flip rather than a layout.
  setLocale(initial.locale);

  if (typeof window === 'undefined' || !window.matchMedia) return () => {};

  const mediaQuery = window.matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)');
  const listener = (): void => {
    const current = useThemeStore.getState().settings;
    if (current.followSystem) {
      const nextResolved = resolveEffectiveTheme(current);
      useThemeStore.setState({ resolvedTheme: nextResolved });
      applyThemeToDocument(nextResolved, current.customAccentId);
    }
  };

  mediaQuery.addEventListener('change', listener);
  return () => mediaQuery.removeEventListener('change', listener);
}

/**
 * The budgets the credentials endpoints run under.
 *
 * Here rather than in the controller so the self-check can read the real
 * numbers instead of a copy of them: a limit that drifts from the one under
 * test is a limit nobody is testing.
 */
import type { RateLimitOptions } from '@betweenus/nest-common';

/**
 * Login and register share one budget per client address: a credential-stuffing
 * run that alternates between them gets no extra room. Generous enough that a
 * person typo-ing their password never sees it.
 */
export const CREDENTIALS_RATE_LIMIT: RateLimitOptions = {
  limit: 20,
  windowSeconds: 60,
  name: 'auth-credentials',
};

/**
 * Login carries a second budget, counted against the account being tried rather
 * than the address trying it.
 *
 * The address limit is the wrong shape for the attack that matters: a botnet
 * spread over a thousand hosts gets 20 attempts a minute *each* against one
 * password, and never trips it. Ten a minute against one email is far more than
 * a person mistyping their own password will ever need, and far less than a
 * guessing run needs to be worth starting.
 *
 * A wrong email is its own bucket, so this cannot be used to lock somebody out
 * of their account for longer than the minute it is aimed at - and the address
 * doing the aiming runs out first anyway.
 *
 * Normalised the way the lookup normalises it, or the bucket is a formality:
 * `Ayaan@x.com` and `ayaan@x.com` reach the same row and would otherwise get
 * ten attempts each. What it cannot do is join up the two *names* for one
 * account - the field takes an email or a username, and telling which account a
 * username belongs to is a database read this runs before.
 *
 * ponytail: a counter is the whole of it. There is no "this account is under
 * attack" signal, no notification and no escalating backoff.
 */
export const LOGIN_RATE_LIMIT: RateLimitOptions = {
  ...CREDENTIALS_RATE_LIMIT,
  subject: (body) => (typeof body.email === 'string' ? body.email.trim().toLowerCase() : null),
  subjectLimit: 10,
};

/**
 * Changing a password, and spending a refresh token.
 *
 * Both are behind a token already, so neither is a way in from nothing - but
 * `POST account/password` checks the current password before it accepts a new
 * one, which makes it an oracle for anybody holding a stolen access token, and
 * a refresh is a database write anyone with a valid token can ask for as fast
 * as they like. Its own bucket rather than the credentials one, so a shared
 * address running out of login budget does not stop a person changing their
 * password.
 */
export const SESSION_RATE_LIMIT: RateLimitOptions = {
  limit: 20,
  windowSeconds: 60,
  name: 'auth-session',
};

# Cloudflare Tunnel ingress for BetweenUs.
#
# BetweenUs is one public hostname. Everything a client needs - REST, /ws/chat,
# /ws/presence, /ws/call, /ws/remote and uploaded files - is behind the Nginx
# gateway on 8080, so this file has one real rule in it.
#
# There are two ways to run the tunnel, and BetweenUs works with either.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. A tunnel you already run on the host (the common case)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# If cloudflared is already a service on this machine - one tunnel for the whole
# server, with other things behind it - do not start the container. Add BetweenUs's
# hostname to the ingress list you already have; it is one entry:
#
#   ingress:
#     - hostname: betweenus.example.com
#       service: http://localhost:8080
#     # ...your other hostnames...
#     - service: http_status:404
#
# Then reload it (`systemctl reload cloudflared`, or restart the service). The
# compose file publishes the gateway on the host as ${GATEWAY_PORT:-8080}, which
# is what `http://localhost:8080` above reaches. Nothing else has to change, and
# no other container is published.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. The tunnel as a container, alongside the stack
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
#   CLOUDFLARE_TUNNEL_TOKEN=... docker compose \
#     -f infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml --profile public up -d
#
# Token mode carries its own ingress rules (they live in the Cloudflare
# dashboard, not here) and the container reaches Nginx as `http://nginx:8080` on
# the internal network - so with a container tunnel the host port does not have
# to be published at all.
#
# To run the container in config-file mode instead, mount this file at
# /etc/cloudflared/config.yml with a credentials file beside it and drop the
# TUNNEL_TOKEN. The service name below is the container, not localhost.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# What does NOT go through the tunnel
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# Voice, video, screen share and remote-desktop *media*, and this is the point
# the whole design turns on rather than a caveat.
#
# A Cloudflare Tunnel carries HTTP and WebSocket. WebRTC media is UDP, and no
# tunnel carries that. The old design ran an SFU, so media had to get past the
# tunnel somehow: a routable address for the SFU to advertise, published TCP and
# UDP ports, and finally a TURN relay. Every one of those was a thing to get
# wrong, and getting it wrong looked like a call that connected and then went
# silent.
#
# Media is now peer to peer, so it never comes near this tunnel. What crosses
# here is signalling - the roster, and the offers, answers and ICE candidates
# two clients exchange - which is a WebSocket, which is exactly what a tunnel is
# good at. Nothing else has to reach this host at all:
#
#   * No port is published for media, in this file or in docker-compose.yml.
#   * No service advertises an address, so there is none to be wrong.
#   * Peers find each other with STUN, which they dial out to themselves.
#   * The pairs of networks that cannot manage a direct path need a TURN relay,
#     which is optional, off by default, and reached outbound by both ends - so
#     even that opens no port here.
#
# This file having one rule in it is the result, not a simplification of it.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A TURN relay cannot be put behind this tunnel
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# It is the obvious thought - the tunnel already publishes this host without a
# port forward, so publish coturn through it too - and it does not work.
#
# The edge terminates TLS for a proxied hostname and expects HTTP inside it.
# TURN over TLS is its own binary protocol, not HTTP, so a client dialling
# turns:betweenus.example.com:443 is refused at the edge and never reaches
# coturn. An ingress rule of `service: tcp://...` does not change that: those
# are reached with `cloudflared access` or WARP on the *client* side, and a
# browser's WebRTC stack cannot run either. Arbitrary TCP for ordinary public
# clients is Cloudflare Spectrum, an Enterprise product.
#
# So a relay lives somewhere with a public address of its own - a small VM is
# enough, since it forwards packets it has no key for. It is configured in .env
# (TURN_URLS) and adds no rule to this file, because the peers dial it outbound
# rather than it being published from here.

tunnel: betweenus
credentials-file: /etc/cloudflared/betweenus.json

# Cloudflare terminates TLS. Nginx behind it speaks plain HTTP on 8080 and
# trusts the X-Forwarded-* headers cloudflared sets.
ingress:
  - hostname: betweenus.example.com
    # `nginx` inside the compose network; `localhost` for a host-run tunnel.
    service: http://nginx:8080
    originRequest:
      # Long-lived sockets: /ws/chat, /ws/presence, /ws/call and /ws/remote all
      # stay open far longer than a request does.
      connectTimeout: 30s
      noTLSVerify: false
      # Uploads stream through; buffering a 100 MB attachment helps nobody.
      disableChunkedEncoding: false

  # Everything that is not BetweenUs's hostname is not BetweenUs's problem.
  - service: http_status:404

# Full stack. Development uses docker-compose.dev.yml (data stores only) plus
# `pnpm dev` on the host; this file runs everything in containers.
#
#   docker compose -f infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml up -d --build
#
# Networks are segmented so only the services that need a data store can reach
# it. Postgres and Redis publish no ports.

name: betweenus

x-service-env: &service-env
  NODE_ENV: production
  LOG_LEVEL: ${LOG_LEVEL:-info}
  DATABASE_URL: postgresql://${POSTGRES_USER:-postgres}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-postgres}@postgres:5432/${POSTGRES_DB:-betweenus}?schema=public
  REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
  # A secret can arrive as a value or as the path of a file holding one. The
  # `_FILE` form is what Docker and Podman secrets, Kubernetes projected volumes
  # and systemd credentials all produce, and it keeps the secret out of
  # `docker inspect` and out of the environment of every process a service
  # spawns. docker-compose.secrets.yml is a ready override that mounts a
  # directory of them; see .env.example.
  #
  # There is no `:?` here any more, because compose cannot say "this one or that
  # one". The services refuse to boot on a missing or placeholder signing secret
  # and name both forms when they do, which is the check that was doing the work
  # regardless.
  JWT_SECRET: ${JWT_SECRET:-}
  JWT_SECRET_FILE: ${JWT_SECRET_FILE:-}
  JWT_REFRESH_SECRET: ${JWT_REFRESH_SECRET:-}
  JWT_REFRESH_SECRET_FILE: ${JWT_REFRESH_SECRET_FILE:-}
  # The secrets from before the last rotation, accepted on the way in and never
  # used to sign. Set for as long as a token signed with the old one can still
  # be presented, then removed - removing them is what ends the rotation.
  JWT_SECRET_PREVIOUS: ${JWT_SECRET_PREVIOUS:-}
  JWT_SECRET_PREVIOUS_FILE: ${JWT_SECRET_PREVIOUS_FILE:-}
  JWT_REFRESH_SECRET_PREVIOUS: ${JWT_REFRESH_SECRET_PREVIOUS:-}
  JWT_REFRESH_SECRET_PREVIOUS_FILE: ${JWT_REFRESH_SECRET_PREVIOUS_FILE:-}
  # Grace for a refresh interrupted between the server rotating and the client
  # storing the result; see .env.example.
  REFRESH_REPLAY_GRACE_MS: ${REFRESH_REPLAY_GRACE_MS:-30000}
  # Seals OAuth client secrets at rest; falls back to JWT_SECRET when unset.
  SETTINGS_SECRET: ${SETTINGS_SECRET:-}
  SETTINGS_SECRET_FILE: ${SETTINGS_SECRET_FILE:-}
  SETTINGS_SECRET_PREVIOUS: ${SETTINGS_SECRET_PREVIOUS:-}
  SETTINGS_SECRET_PREVIOUS_FILE: ${SETTINGS_SECRET_PREVIOUS_FILE:-}
  # Where a browser reaches this deployment - the OAuth callback is built from it.
  PUBLIC_API_URL: ${PUBLIC_API_URL:-http://localhost:8080}
  CORS_ORIGIN: ${CORS_ORIGIN:-*}
  # Empty S3 values keep uploads on the local volume mounted below.
  STORAGE_DRIVER: ${STORAGE_DRIVER:-}
  LOCAL_STORAGE_PATH: /data/uploads
  MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES: ${MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES:-26214400}
  MAX_ATTACHMENT_BYTES: ${MAX_ATTACHMENT_BYTES:-104857600}
  MAX_PICTURE_BYTES: ${MAX_PICTURE_BYTES:-8388608}
  S3_ENDPOINT: ${S3_ENDPOINT:-}
  S3_BUCKET: ${S3_BUCKET:-}
  S3_REGION: ${S3_REGION:-us-east-1}
  S3_ACCESS_KEY: ${S3_ACCESS_KEY:-}
  S3_SECRET_KEY: ${S3_SECRET_KEY:-}
  S3_PUBLIC_URL: ${S3_PUBLIC_URL:-}
  # Firebase Cloud Messaging, for the Android push. Empty = push is off, which
  # is a running deployment without notifications rather than a broken one.
  FIREBASE_PROJECT_ID: ${FIREBASE_PROJECT_ID:-}
  FIREBASE_CLIENT_EMAIL: ${FIREBASE_CLIENT_EMAIL:-}
  FIREBASE_PRIVATE_KEY: ${FIREBASE_PRIVATE_KEY:-}
  FIREBASE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT: ${FIREBASE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT:-}

# Everything the backup script needs: it reaches Postgres over the data network
# with the same credentials the services use, and writes where BACKUP_DATA_PATH
# points. `pg_dump` comes from the postgres image so its version matches the
# server's - a dump taken by a newer or older client is the classic way to find
# out, during a restore, that the backup was never usable.
x-backup: &backup
  image: postgres:16-alpine
  environment:
    PGHOST: postgres
    PGUSER: ${POSTGRES_USER:-postgres}
    PGPASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-postgres}
    PGDATABASE: ${POSTGRES_DB:-betweenus}
    BACKUP_DIR: /backups
    # Weekly, and eight kept - two months of history for a few megabytes of
    # gzipped SQL. The interval is in hours: 24 is nightly, 1 is hourly.
    BACKUP_INTERVAL_HOURS: ${BACKUP_INTERVAL_HOURS:-168}
    BACKUP_KEEP: ${BACKUP_KEEP:-8}
    BACKUP_ON_MIGRATE: ${BACKUP_ON_MIGRATE:-1}
    # Off the host. Empty bucket means off, and nothing else here is read - see
    # backup.sh. A dump beside the database it came from covers a bad migration
    # and not a dead disk.
    BACKUP_S3_ENDPOINT: ${BACKUP_S3_ENDPOINT:-}
    BACKUP_S3_BUCKET: ${BACKUP_S3_BUCKET:-}
    BACKUP_S3_PREFIX: ${BACKUP_S3_PREFIX:-betweenus}
    BACKUP_S3_REGION: ${BACKUP_S3_REGION:-us-east-1}
    BACKUP_S3_ACCESS_KEY: ${BACKUP_S3_ACCESS_KEY:-}
    BACKUP_S3_SECRET_KEY: ${BACKUP_S3_SECRET_KEY:-}
    BACKUP_OFFSITE_REQUIRED: ${BACKUP_OFFSITE_REQUIRED:-0}
  entrypoint: ["/bin/sh", "/usr/local/bin/backup.sh"]
  volumes:
    - ./backup.sh:/usr/local/bin/backup.sh:ro
    - ${BACKUP_DATA_PATH:-backup-data}:/backups
  networks:
    - data-network

services:
  nginx:
    image: nginx:1.27-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      # Published on the host so a cloudflared already running there - one
      # tunnel for the whole server - can point at http://localhost:8080. With
      # the container tunnel below this does not need to be published at all;
      # set GATEWAY_PORT to 127.0.0.1:8080 to keep it off the LAN.
      - "${GATEWAY_PORT:-8080}:8080"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "wget -q -O- http://127.0.0.1:8080/health || exit 1"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 12
    volumes:
      - ../nginx/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro
    depends_on:
      - auth-service
      - server-service
      - chat-service
      - call-service
      - presence-service
      - notification-service
      - remote-gateway
      - admin-web
      - web
    networks:
      - cloudflare-network
      - api-network
      - remote-network

  # The web client: static bundle behind the same gateway, served at its root.
  # No API of its own - it calls the same services the desktop app does.
  web:
    build:
      context: ../..
      dockerfile: infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile
      target: web
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks:
      - api-network

  # The admin panel: static bundle behind the same gateway.
  admin-web:
    build:
      context: ../..
      dockerfile: infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile
      target: admin-web
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks:
      - api-network

  # Public ingress, opt-in:
  #   docker compose -f infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml --profile public up -d
  #
  # Skip it entirely if cloudflared already runs on the host for the whole
  # server: add one ingress entry pointing at http://localhost:${GATEWAY_PORT}
  # and reload it. See infrastructure/cloudflare/tunnel.yml, which documents
  # both ways round.
  cloudflared:
    image: cloudflare/cloudflared:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    command: tunnel --no-autoupdate run
    environment:
      # Left blank when unset: Compose interpolates every service, profile or
      # not, so a required-check here would break plain `up` for anyone whose
      # cloudflared runs on the host. Empty token only fails --profile public,
      # where cloudflared itself reports it.
      TUNNEL_TOKEN: ${CLOUDFLARE_TUNNEL_TOKEN:-}
    depends_on:
      nginx:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - cloudflare-network
    profiles:
      - public

  # One dump, then exit - the safety net for the migration below, which is the
  # one moment a schema change can lose data irreversibly. It runs before
  # `migrate`, and a failed dump stops the migration rather than being logged
  # and ignored; set BACKUP_ON_MIGRATE=0 if you would rather it did not.
  db-backup-once:
    <<: *backup
    restart: "no"
    command: ["once"]
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy

  # The scheduled backup: one dump now, then one every BACKUP_INTERVAL_HOURS.
  # Sleep-and-dump rather than cron because a container that only wakes up
  # hourly is a container whose failures nobody sees in `docker compose logs`.
  db-backup:
    <<: *backup
    restart: unless-stopped
    command: ["loop"]
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      # After the pre-migration dump, not alongside it. Both used to wait on
      # the same healthy Postgres and start together, which meant two dumps of
      # the same database in the same second - one of them redundant, and the
      # pair of them racing. The scratch-file collision that caused is fixed in
      # backup.sh; taking the same dump twice was never wanted either.
      #
      # Nothing is lost by waiting: if the pre-migration dump fails, `migrate`
      # does not run and no service starts, so a scheduled backup of a stack
      # that is not up would be backing up nothing anyone is using.
      db-backup-once:
        condition: service_completed_successfully

  # One-shot: applies Prisma migrations before any service accepts traffic.
  # Reuses the auth-service image because it already carries the schema and the
  # Prisma CLI; nothing about it is auth-specific.
  migrate:
    build:
      context: ../..
      dockerfile: infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile
      target: auth-service
    restart: "no"
    # Prisma verifies it can write to its engine directory; the image's `node`
    # user cannot. Nothing else runs as root.
    user: root
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://${POSTGRES_USER:-postgres}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-postgres}@postgres:5432/${POSTGRES_DB:-betweenus}?schema=public
    working_dir: /repo/packages/database
    command: ["./node_modules/.bin/prisma", "migrate", "deploy"]
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      db-backup-once:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    networks:
      - data-network

  auth-service:
    build:
      context: ../..
      dockerfile: infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile
      target: auth-service
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      <<: *service-env
      AUTH_SERVICE_PORT: 3001
    depends_on:
      migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - api-network
      - data-network

  server-service:
    build:
      context: ../..
      dockerfile: infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile
      target: server-service
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      <<: *service-env
      SERVER_SERVICE_PORT: 3003
    depends_on:
      migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - api-network
      - data-network

  chat-service:
    build:
      context: ../..
      dockerfile: infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile
      target: chat-service
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      <<: *service-env
      CHAT_SERVICE_PORT: 3004
    volumes:
      # Uploads survive container replacement when the local driver is active.
      # UPLOAD_DATA_PATH takes either a Docker volume name (the default) or a
      # host path - `/mnt/disk2/betweenus-uploads`, `D:/betweenus-uploads` - to keep
      # the files somewhere you can see and back up.
      #
      # The service runs as uid 1000, and the image ships /data/uploads owned by
      # it so an empty named volume inherits that. A *host* path is never seeded
      # from the image: chown it to 1000:1000 first, or every attachment fails
      # with EACCES while the rest of the service works perfectly.
      - ${UPLOAD_DATA_PATH:-upload-data}:/data/uploads
    depends_on:
      migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - api-network
      - data-network

  notification-service:
    build:
      context: ../..
      dockerfile: infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile
      target: notification-service
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      <<: *service-env
      NOTIFICATION_SERVICE_PORT: 3006
    depends_on:
      migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - api-network
      - data-network

  presence-service:
    build:
      context: ../..
      dockerfile: infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile
      target: presence-service
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      <<: *service-env
      PRESENCE_SERVICE_PORT: 3005
    depends_on:
      migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - api-network
      - data-network

  call-service:
    build:
      context: ../..
      dockerfile: infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile
      target: call-service
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      <<: *service-env
      CALL_SERVICE_PORT: 3007
      # There is no media-server address here, and there must never be one:
      # call-service introduces two clients over /ws/call and they carry the
      # media between themselves. See section 4 of claude.md.
      #
      # Where a peer learns its own public address. Not a relay, needs no port
      # opened, and one request per call is all the traffic; point it at your
      # own coturn if you would rather not talk to these.
      STUN_URLS: ${STUN_URLS:-stun:stun.l.google.com:19302,stun:stun.cloudflare.com:3478}
      # A relay, for the pairs of networks that cannot form a direct path at all
      # - symmetric NAT on both sides, mobile carrier-grade NAT. Optional and
      # unset by default, so this deployment relays nothing unless you say so;
      # the cost of leaving it off is that those particular calls fail. The key
      # never leaves this service - only the short-lived credentials it mints.
      # The relay this deployment runs, for the pairs of networks STUN cannot
      # join directly. All three together, or it is ignored: the relay needs a
      # reachable address of its own - a small VM, not this host behind the tunnel.
      TURN_URLS: ${TURN_URLS:-}
      TURN_USERNAME: ${TURN_USERNAME:-}
      TURN_CREDENTIAL: ${TURN_CREDENTIAL:-}
    depends_on:
      migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - api-network
      - data-network

  # Remote desktop, kept off every network it does not need. It talks to
  # Postgres and to nothing else; it never reaches the chat services, and
  # nothing reaches the machines - their agents dial out.
  remote-gateway:
    build:
      context: ../..
      dockerfile: infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile
      target: remote-gateway
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      <<: *service-env
      REMOTE_GATEWAY_PORT: 3008
      # The same answer call-service gives, for the same reason: the agent and
      # the controller have to find each other, and nothing here knows or needs
      # to know where either of them is.
      STUN_URLS: ${STUN_URLS:-stun:stun.l.google.com:19302,stun:stun.cloudflare.com:3478}
      # The relay this deployment runs, for the pairs of networks STUN cannot
      # join directly. All three together, or it is ignored: the relay needs a
      # reachable address of its own - a small VM, not this host behind the tunnel.
      TURN_URLS: ${TURN_URLS:-}
      TURN_USERNAME: ${TURN_USERNAME:-}
      TURN_CREDENTIAL: ${TURN_CREDENTIAL:-}
    depends_on:
      migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      # Redis carries the session relay: the agent and the controller need not
      # be on the same replica, so the messages between them go through Pub/Sub.
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - remote-network
      - data-network

  # There was a `livekit` service here, and it is worth knowing what went with
  # it. It published 7880, 7881 and a UDP range, because WebRTC media cannot go
  # through Nginx or a Cloudflare Tunnel. It needed LIVEKIT_NODE_IP - the
  # address clients reach this host on - because otherwise it advertised its
  # Docker bridge address and every call negotiated all the way to media and
  # then timed out. That setting had no right answer for every deployment and a
  # wrong one was invisible until somebody tried to talk.
  #
  # Media now goes directly between the clients. No container carries it, no
  # port is published for it, and nothing in this file states an address that
  # only the server can reach. Adding a media service back is how all three of
  # those come back together.

  postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER:-postgres}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-postgres}
      POSTGRES_DB: ${POSTGRES_DB:-betweenus}
    volumes:
      # POSTGRES_DATA_PATH is a Docker volume name by default and a host path
      # when scripts/data-path.mjs has written one. Postgres chowns its own
      # data directory on start, so a bind mount needs nothing done to it.
      - ${POSTGRES_DATA_PATH:-postgres-data}:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U ${POSTGRES_USER:-postgres}"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 20
    networks:
      - data-network

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - ${REDIS_DATA_PATH:-redis-data}:/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 20
    networks:
      - data-network

volumes:
  postgres-data:
  redis-data:
  upload-data:
  backup-data:

networks:
  cloudflare-network:
  api-network:
  data-network:
  # There is no media-network: no container carries media.
  #
  # Remote desktop is deliberately not on api-network: the gateway reaches
  # Postgres and nothing else reaches it except Nginx.
  remote-network:

# Development-only infrastructure.
# Runs the stateful dependencies so developers do not install Postgres/Redis locally.
# Application services run on the host with `pnpm dev`.
#
# Usage:
#   pnpm dev:infra        (docker compose --env-file .env -f ... up -d)
#   pnpm dev:infra:down
#
# The `--env-file .env` matters: compose reads `.env` from *this* directory, not
# from the repo root, so without it every `${VAR}` below comes up empty.

name: betweenus-dev

services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    container_name: betweenus-dev-postgres
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER:-postgres}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-postgres}
      POSTGRES_DB: ${POSTGRES_DB:-betweenus}
    ports:
      # Exposed on localhost only - never bind 0.0.0.0 for a database.
      - "127.0.0.1:5432:5432"
    volumes:
      - postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U ${POSTGRES_USER:-postgres} -d ${POSTGRES_DB:-betweenus}"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 20

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    container_name: betweenus-dev-redis
    restart: unless-stopped
    command: ["redis-server", "--appendonly", "no"]
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:6379:6379"
    volumes:
      - redis-data:/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 20

  # There is no media container here any more. There used to be an SFU, and it
  # needed a node IP, two published TCP ports and a published UDP range, none of
  # which a developer could get right on the first try - see the note in
  # docker-compose.yml. Calls in development now go directly between the two
  # clients, so `pnpm dev:infra` is Postgres and Redis and nothing else.

volumes:
  postgres-data:
  redis-data:

# Secrets as files, layered over either stack.
#
#   docker compose --env-file .env \
#     -f infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml \
#     -f infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.secrets.yml up -d
#
# WHAT THIS IS FOR
#
# `.env` is where a secret goes when there is nowhere better. It is one file
# holding every secret this deployment has; its contents are in the environment
# of every process a service spawns, in `docker inspect`, and in whatever backup
# takes the host's home directory. Phase 27 made a placeholder `JWT_SECRET`
# refuse to boot and gave nobody anywhere better to put the real one. This is
# the somewhere better that costs nothing to adopt.
#
# HOW
#
# `SECRETS_PATH` is a directory of one-secret-per-file, mounted read-only at
# /run/secrets in every service. Each `NAME_FILE` names a path inside it, and
# `@betweenus/config` reads the file when `NAME` itself is unset. Nothing else
# in the stack changes: the same variable names, the same boot checks.
#
#   mkdir -p /etc/betweenus/secrets && chmod 700 /etc/betweenus/secrets
#   node -e "console.log(require('crypto').randomBytes(48).toString('hex'))" \
#     > /etc/betweenus/secrets/jwt_secret
#   node -e "console.log(require('crypto').randomBytes(48).toString('hex'))" \
#     > /etc/betweenus/secrets/jwt_refresh_secret
#   chmod 400 /etc/betweenus/secrets/*
#   echo 'SECRETS_PATH=/etc/betweenus/secrets' >> .env
#
# Then take JWT_SECRET and JWT_REFRESH_SECRET out of `.env` entirely. A value
# still there wins over the file, which is what makes adopting this reversible
# and what makes a half-done migration confusing - so finish it.
#
# ROTATING
#
#   cp jwt_secret jwt_secret_previous
#   node -e "..." > jwt_secret
#   docker compose ... up -d
#
# Sessions signed with the old secret keep verifying because
# `JWT_SECRET_PREVIOUS_FILE` names it. Delete jwt_secret_previous and restart
# once no token can still carry the old signature - one access-token lifetime
# for `jwt_secret`, and the refresh lifetime for `jwt_refresh_secret`. Deleting
# it is what ends the rotation; leaving it there forever means two live secrets.
#
# `settings_secret` seals the OAuth client secrets in the database. Rotating it
# with a `_previous` beside it lets them be read and re-sealed; rotating it
# without one makes every stored one unreadable, and unreadable comes back from
# the admin panel as an empty field rather than as an error.
#
# NOT A VAULT
#
# This is files on a host with file permissions, which is the correct next step
# after `.env` and is not centralised secret storage. A deployment that wants
# Vault or a cloud secrets manager points its agent at the same directory and
# nothing here changes - which is the point of the indirection.

x-secret-files: &secret-files
  JWT_SECRET_FILE: /run/secrets/jwt_secret
  JWT_REFRESH_SECRET_FILE: /run/secrets/jwt_refresh_secret
  JWT_SECRET_PREVIOUS_FILE: /run/secrets/jwt_secret_previous
  JWT_REFRESH_SECRET_PREVIOUS_FILE: /run/secrets/jwt_refresh_secret_previous
  SETTINGS_SECRET_FILE: /run/secrets/settings_secret
  SETTINGS_SECRET_PREVIOUS_FILE: /run/secrets/settings_secret_previous

x-secrets-mount: &secrets-mount
  - ${SECRETS_PATH:?SECRETS_PATH must point at the directory holding the secret files}:/run/secrets:ro

# A path naming a file that is not there is not an error: `@betweenus/config`
# only reads `NAME_FILE` when `NAME` is unset, and only complains when the file
# it was told to read is unreadable. So the four `_previous` paths above name
# files that exist only during a rotation - and `SETTINGS_SECRET` remains
# optional, falling back to `JWT_SECRET` exactly as it did before.
services:
  auth-service:
    environment: *secret-files
    volumes: *secrets-mount
  server-service:
    environment: *secret-files
    volumes: *secrets-mount
  # chat-service already mounts the upload volume; compose merges the two lists
  # by container path, so this adds to it rather than replacing it.
  chat-service:
    environment: *secret-files
    volumes: *secrets-mount
  notification-service:
    environment: *secret-files
    volumes: *secrets-mount
  presence-service:
    environment: *secret-files
    volumes: *secrets-mount
  call-service:
    environment: *secret-files
    volumes: *secrets-mount
  remote-gateway:
    environment: *secret-files
    volumes: *secrets-mount

# The stack, pulled rather than built. docker-compose.build.yml is the same
# stack built from this checkout instead - for working on it, or for running a
# commit no release was ever cut from.
#
#   docker compose --env-file .env \
#     -f infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml pull
#   docker compose --env-file .env \
#     -f infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml up -d
#
# Every image comes from one Docker Hub repository, told apart by a tag prefix:
# aiyuayaan/betweenus:chat-service-0.0.1. BETWEENUS_VERSION picks which release
# runs; leave it unset and each service tracks the moving `latest` tag, or set
# it to `alpha` or `beta` to track a channel.
#
# WHY THIS FILE EXISTS ALONGSIDE docker-compose.build.yml, AND WHAT MUST NOT
# DIVERGE
#
# `name`, the service names, the volume names and the environment are the ones
# docker-compose.build.yml uses, and they have to stay that way. Compose derives
# volume names from the project name - betweenus_postgres-data - so a project
# renamed here is a deployment that comes up with an empty database beside the
# full one it can no longer see. Nothing about switching from building to
# pulling is allowed to touch where the data lives.
#
# Which makes the move from a built deployment to a pulled one exactly one
# thing: swap the -f, same .env, same host. Same volumes, same data.

name: betweenus

x-service-env: &service-env
  NODE_ENV: production
  LOG_LEVEL: ${LOG_LEVEL:-info}
  DATABASE_URL: postgresql://${POSTGRES_USER:-postgres}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-postgres}@postgres:5432/${POSTGRES_DB:-betweenus}?schema=public
  REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
  # A secret can arrive as a value or as the path of a file holding one. The
  # `_FILE` form is what Docker and Podman secrets, Kubernetes projected volumes
  # and systemd credentials all produce, and it keeps the secret out of
  # `docker inspect` and out of the environment of every process a service
  # spawns. docker-compose.secrets.yml is a ready override that mounts a
  # directory of them; see .env.example.
  #
  # There is no `:?` here any more, because compose cannot say "this one or that
  # one". The services refuse to boot on a missing or placeholder signing secret
  # and name both forms when they do, which is the check that was doing the work
  # regardless.
  JWT_SECRET: ${JWT_SECRET:-}
  JWT_SECRET_FILE: ${JWT_SECRET_FILE:-}
  JWT_REFRESH_SECRET: ${JWT_REFRESH_SECRET:-}
  JWT_REFRESH_SECRET_FILE: ${JWT_REFRESH_SECRET_FILE:-}
  # The secrets from before the last rotation, accepted on the way in and never
  # used to sign. Set for as long as a token signed with the old one can still
  # be presented, then removed - removing them is what ends the rotation.
  JWT_SECRET_PREVIOUS: ${JWT_SECRET_PREVIOUS:-}
  JWT_SECRET_PREVIOUS_FILE: ${JWT_SECRET_PREVIOUS_FILE:-}
  JWT_REFRESH_SECRET_PREVIOUS: ${JWT_REFRESH_SECRET_PREVIOUS:-}
  JWT_REFRESH_SECRET_PREVIOUS_FILE: ${JWT_REFRESH_SECRET_PREVIOUS_FILE:-}
  REFRESH_REPLAY_GRACE_MS: ${REFRESH_REPLAY_GRACE_MS:-30000}
  SETTINGS_SECRET: ${SETTINGS_SECRET:-}
  SETTINGS_SECRET_FILE: ${SETTINGS_SECRET_FILE:-}
  SETTINGS_SECRET_PREVIOUS: ${SETTINGS_SECRET_PREVIOUS:-}
  SETTINGS_SECRET_PREVIOUS_FILE: ${SETTINGS_SECRET_PREVIOUS_FILE:-}
  PUBLIC_API_URL: ${PUBLIC_API_URL:-http://localhost:8080}
  CORS_ORIGIN: ${CORS_ORIGIN:-*}
  STORAGE_DRIVER: ${STORAGE_DRIVER:-}
  LOCAL_STORAGE_PATH: /data/uploads
  MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES: ${MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES:-26214400}

x-backup: &backup
  image: postgres:16-alpine
  environment:
    PGHOST: postgres
    PGUSER: ${POSTGRES_USER:-postgres}
    PGPASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-postgres}
    PGDATABASE: ${POSTGRES_DB:-betweenus}
    BACKUP_DIR: /backups
    BACKUP_INTERVAL_HOURS: ${BACKUP_INTERVAL_HOURS:-168}
    BACKUP_KEEP: ${BACKUP_KEEP:-8}
    BACKUP_ON_MIGRATE: ${BACKUP_ON_MIGRATE:-1}
    # Off the host. Empty bucket means off, and nothing else here is read - see
    # backup.sh. A dump beside the database it came from covers a bad migration
    # and not a dead disk.
    BACKUP_S3_ENDPOINT: ${BACKUP_S3_ENDPOINT:-}
    BACKUP_S3_BUCKET: ${BACKUP_S3_BUCKET:-}
    BACKUP_S3_PREFIX: ${BACKUP_S3_PREFIX:-betweenus}
    BACKUP_S3_REGION: ${BACKUP_S3_REGION:-us-east-1}
    BACKUP_S3_ACCESS_KEY: ${BACKUP_S3_ACCESS_KEY:-}
    BACKUP_S3_SECRET_KEY: ${BACKUP_S3_SECRET_KEY:-}
    BACKUP_OFFSITE_REQUIRED: ${BACKUP_OFFSITE_REQUIRED:-0}
  entrypoint: ["/bin/sh", "/usr/local/bin/backup.sh"]
  volumes:
    - ./backup.sh:/usr/local/bin/backup.sh:ro
    - ${BACKUP_DATA_PATH:-backup-data}:/backups

services:
  nginx:
    image: nginx:1.27-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "${GATEWAY_PORT:-8080}:8080"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "wget -q -O- http://127.0.0.1:8080/health || exit 1"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 12
    volumes:
      - ../nginx/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro
    depends_on:
      - auth-service
      - server-service
      - chat-service
      - call-service
      - presence-service
      - notification-service
      - remote-gateway
      - admin-web
      - web
    networks:
      - cloudflare-network
      - api-network
      - remote-network

  web:
    image: ${BETWEENUS_IMAGE_REPO:-aiyuayaan/betweenus}:web-${BETWEENUS_VERSION:-latest}
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks:
      - api-network

  admin-web:
    image: ${BETWEENUS_IMAGE_REPO:-aiyuayaan/betweenus}:admin-web-${BETWEENUS_VERSION:-latest}
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks:
      - api-network

  cloudflared:
    image: cloudflare/cloudflared:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    command: tunnel --no-autoupdate run
    environment:
      TUNNEL_TOKEN: ${CLOUDFLARE_TUNNEL_TOKEN:-}
    depends_on:
      nginx:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - cloudflare-network
    profiles:
      - public

  db-backup-once:
    <<: *backup
    restart: "no"
    command: ["once"]
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy

  db-backup:
    <<: *backup
    restart: unless-stopped
    command: ["loop"]
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      # After the pre-migration dump, not alongside it. Both used to wait on
      # the same healthy Postgres and start together, which meant two dumps of
      # the same database in the same second - one of them redundant, and the
      # pair of them racing. The scratch-file collision that caused is fixed in
      # backup.sh; taking the same dump twice was never wanted either.
      #
      # Nothing is lost by waiting: if the pre-migration dump fails, `migrate`
      # does not run and no service starts, so a scheduled backup of a stack
      # that is not up would be backing up nothing anyone is using.
      db-backup-once:
        condition: service_completed_successfully

  # Same image as auth-service, which is where the Prisma schema and the CLI
  # live. Pulling rather than building changes nothing about the ordering: the
  # dump runs, then the migration, then anything that serves traffic.
  migrate:
    image: ${BETWEENUS_IMAGE_REPO:-aiyuayaan/betweenus}:auth-service-${BETWEENUS_VERSION:-latest}
    restart: "no"
    user: root
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://${POSTGRES_USER:-postgres}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-postgres}@postgres:5432/${POSTGRES_DB:-betweenus}?schema=public
    working_dir: /repo/packages/database
    command: ["./node_modules/.bin/prisma", "migrate", "deploy"]
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      db-backup-once:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    networks:
      - data-network

  auth-service:
    image: ${BETWEENUS_IMAGE_REPO:-aiyuayaan/betweenus}:auth-service-${BETWEENUS_VERSION:-latest}
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      <<: *service-env
      AUTH_SERVICE_PORT: 3001
    depends_on:
      migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - api-network
      - data-network

  server-service:
    image: ${BETWEENUS_IMAGE_REPO:-aiyuayaan/betweenus}:server-service-${BETWEENUS_VERSION:-latest}
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      <<: *service-env
      SERVER_SERVICE_PORT: 3003
    depends_on:
      migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - api-network
      - data-network

  chat-service:
    image: ${BETWEENUS_IMAGE_REPO:-aiyuayaan/betweenus}:chat-service-${BETWEENUS_VERSION:-latest}
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      <<: *service-env
      CHAT_SERVICE_PORT: 3004
    volumes:
      # Same mount, same default volume name, same uid expectation as the built
      # stack. A host path here still has to be chowned to 1000:1000 first.
      - ${UPLOAD_DATA_PATH:-upload-data}:/data/uploads
    depends_on:
      migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - api-network
      - data-network

  notification-service:
    image: ${BETWEENUS_IMAGE_REPO:-aiyuayaan/betweenus}:notification-service-${BETWEENUS_VERSION:-latest}
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      <<: *service-env
      NOTIFICATION_SERVICE_PORT: 3006
    depends_on:
      migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - api-network
      - data-network

  presence-service:
    image: ${BETWEENUS_IMAGE_REPO:-aiyuayaan/betweenus}:presence-service-${BETWEENUS_VERSION:-latest}
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      <<: *service-env
      PRESENCE_SERVICE_PORT: 3005
    depends_on:
      migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - api-network
      - data-network

  call-service:
    image: ${BETWEENUS_IMAGE_REPO:-aiyuayaan/betweenus}:call-service-${BETWEENUS_VERSION:-latest}
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      <<: *service-env
      CALL_SERVICE_PORT: 3007
      # Still no media-server address, for the reason section 4 of claude.md
      # gives. Pulling an image instead of building one changes nothing about
      # where media goes: directly between the peers, never through here.
      STUN_URLS: ${STUN_URLS:-stun:stun.l.google.com:19302,stun:stun.cloudflare.com:3478}
      # The relay this deployment runs, for the pairs of networks STUN cannot
      # join directly. All three together, or it is ignored: the relay needs a
      # reachable address of its own - a small VM, not this host behind the tunnel.
      TURN_URLS: ${TURN_URLS:-}
      TURN_USERNAME: ${TURN_USERNAME:-}
      TURN_CREDENTIAL: ${TURN_CREDENTIAL:-}
    depends_on:
      migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - api-network
      - data-network

  remote-gateway:
    image: ${BETWEENUS_IMAGE_REPO:-aiyuayaan/betweenus}:remote-gateway-${BETWEENUS_VERSION:-latest}
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      <<: *service-env
      REMOTE_GATEWAY_PORT: 3008
      STUN_URLS: ${STUN_URLS:-stun:stun.l.google.com:19302,stun:stun.cloudflare.com:3478}
      # The relay this deployment runs, for the pairs of networks STUN cannot
      # join directly. All three together, or it is ignored: the relay needs a
      # reachable address of its own - a small VM, not this host behind the tunnel.
      TURN_URLS: ${TURN_URLS:-}
      TURN_USERNAME: ${TURN_USERNAME:-}
      TURN_CREDENTIAL: ${TURN_CREDENTIAL:-}
    depends_on:
      migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - remote-network
      - data-network

  postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER:-postgres}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-postgres}
      POSTGRES_DB: ${POSTGRES_DB:-betweenus}
    volumes:
      - ${POSTGRES_DATA_PATH:-postgres-data}:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U ${POSTGRES_USER:-postgres}"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 20
    networks:
      - data-network

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - ${REDIS_DATA_PATH:-redis-data}:/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 20
    networks:
      - data-network

volumes:
  postgres-data:
  redis-data:
  upload-data:
  backup-data:

networks:
  cloudflare-network:
  api-network:
  data-network:
  # No media-network, for the same reason docker-compose.yml has none: no
  # container carries media. Remote desktop stays off api-network.
  remote-network:

# BetweenUs

A modern, secure communication platform with end-to-end encrypted messaging, peer-to-peer (P2P) WebRTC voice/video channels, interactive screen sharing, picture-in-picture, synchronised listening, and remote desktop access. Built as a high-performance pnpm + Turborepo monorepo of NestJS microservices with Desktop (Electron), Web (React), and Native Mobile (Android Jetpack Compose) clients. Messages, attachments, and call media are end-to-end encrypted: the server stores and routes ciphertext, never holding any key that can decrypt it. Voice, video, and screen sharing stream directly between participants via a peer-to-peer WebRTC mesh with DTLS-SRTP encryption — requiring zero media server infrastructure. `CLAUDE.md` is the target architecture. `development/` tracks what is built, why each decision was taken, and what is deliberately left open. `docs/` is the complete documentation suite covering architecture, services, system design, security, and step-by-step deployment with Docker Compose and Cloudflare Tunnels. --- ## Status | Area | State | | --- | --- | | Accounts | Register, login, refresh-token rotation with reuse detection, Google and GitHub sign-in, admin panel | | Servers | Servers, custom roles with colours, per-member permission overrides, invite links that expire and can be revoked, custom emoji, incoming webhooks, server settings | | Channels | Public and private text channels, private channels as an allowlist, direct messages between friends | | Messages & Chat | End-to-end encrypted, realtime over WebSocket, history paging in both directions, replies, `:` emoji search, per-server custom emoji including animated, reactions with who-reacted names, drag-and-drop and a preview before sending, full-screen zoomable image viewer, integrated video player, and local media album saving | | Voice and video | Peer-to-peer voice channels, camera, one screen share at a time with takeover, join and leave tones, manual quality override, end-to-end encrypted media, no media server | | Listen together | A shared YouTube queue inside a voice call: everyone hears the same track in step, from their own connection, at full quality, with the video on screen. Browse the real youtube.com inside the app, signed in as yourself, and queue what you are looking at. Anybody can add, skip or pause; music ducks under whoever is talking. No audio is streamed between anybody | | Play together | Six board games inside a voice call - Tic-tac-toe, Connect Four, Reversi, Dots and Boxes, Ludo, and Carrom with a real physics simulation. One board everybody sees, two chairs anybody can take, and a rematch button. `call-service` referees the moves, so a move is a number on the wire rather than somebody's screen being streamed | | Android Client | Native Jetpack Compose + Material 3 app with E2EE messaging, WhatsApp-style media picker and composer, media viewers, and public gallery saving (`Pictures/BetweenUs`, `Movies/BetweenUs`) | | Presence | Online / idle / do not disturb / invisible, last seen with a three-tier privacy setting, typing indicators, voice rosters | | Profiles | An avatar and a wide cover picture on every account, an about line, a card - hovered on desktop and web, double-tapped on Android - carrying the picture, whether they are here, when they were last here and what their line says, and a full profile screen behind it for the whole line at a size worth reading | | Moments | Photo, video and text posts that disappear after 24 hours, seen by the people you are friends with - a full-screen player with a bar per post, tap to move, hold to pause, a segmented ring around an avatar counting what is unwatched, and a list of who has seen yours. **End-to-end encrypted, with the audience frozen when the post is written**: the key is wrapped once per device of every friend you have at that moment, so somebody who becomes a friend tomorrow does not see today's post | | Webhooks | A URL you give another system so it can post into a channel - a build server, an alerting stack, a `curl` in a deploy script. Discord's request shape, so an integration already pointed at Discord works by changing only the URL. **These messages are the one thing here that is not end-to-end encrypted, and every client says so on every one of them** | | Notifications | Desktop notifications, system tray, start with the system, per-channel and per-person mute, quiet hours, persisted unread with a line that survives a restart | | Remote desktop | A machine offers itself from Settings, dials out to the gateway, and is viewed and driven from another client; per-machine permissions with expiry, and an audit trail | ## Features, and where each one works **Desktop** is the Electron app, **Web** is the same UI in a browser tab (`apps/web` mounts `apps/desktop/src`, so they are one codebase), and **Android** is the native Compose client. Where the three differ it is almost always for one reason: screen capture by source, synthetic mouse and keyboard input and the OS keychain live behind the Electron preload bridge, and a browser tab has none of them.
